decision_observations.support: The opening beatitude, tree image, and Yahweh's closing knowledge of the righteous way form one antithetical wisdom argument.

decision_observations.support: The revolt, heavenly response, royal decree, and warning to rulers are successive voices in one enthronement drama.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 7 is the strongest child opening because I will tell of the decree changes speaker and begins the royal speech; a 1-6/7-12 reading remains plausible.

decision_observations.support: Complaint, shield confession, sleep testimony, rescue cry, and salvation blessing complete a compact lament-to-trust arc.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The Selah after verse 4 could mark a 1-4/5-8 division, yet the sleep testimony carries the trust confession directly into the final plea.

decision_observations.support: The answered opening prayer moves through rebuke, inward trust, communal longing, and peaceful sleep without a stable independent stanza.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 2's address to the sons of men is the strongest speech seam, but separating it would detach the rebuke from the prayer and sleep conclusion.

decision_observations.support: Morning address, moral appeal, temple approach, enemy petition, and refuge blessing all serve the speaker's request to be led.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 7's But as for me could open a worship-and-guidance child after the wicked portrait, though the same enemy pressure governs both halves.

decision_observations.support: The penitential cry accumulates bodily pain, death anxiety, tears, and then confidence that Yahweh has heard.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 8's dismissal of evildoers is a real lament-to-confidence turn, but it depends on the heard prayer of verses 1-7.

decision_observations.support: The innocence protest, appeal for divine judgment, and closing justice testimony answer one accusation.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 10's My shield is with God could begin a justice-hymn child after the judgment plea; the unresolved accusation keeps the full Psalm context necessary.

decision_observations.support: The enveloping Yahweh, our Lord refrain binds cosmic majesty, the humanity question, and delegated creaturely rule.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 4's What is man opens the strongest meditation child, but the question receives its force from the heavens in verses 1-3 and resolves in the verse-9 refrain.

decision_observations.support: Complaint about vanished faithfulness, Yahweh's direct promise, and the closing diagnosis of the wicked complete one communal lament.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 5's Because of the oppression opens a divine oracle, yet verses 6-8 immediately test that promise against the lament's social setting.

decision_observations.support: Repeated How long, direct petition, and rejoicing trust make a deliberately compressed lament progression.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 5's But I trust is a genuine confidence turn, but the two-verse trust close is not independently intelligible without the unanswered questions and petition.

decision_observations.support: The fool portrait, divine inspection, sudden judgment, and Zion salvation wish form one wisdom-lament argument.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 7's salvation wish is the strongest closing child, though its longing answers the corruption and fear described in verses 1-6.

decision_observations.support: The entrance question and the answer's ethical catalogue are a single liturgical exchange.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 2 begins the answer to verse 1, but question and response must remain retrievable together as the entrance liturgy.

decision_observations.support: Petition, rejection of rival loyalties, inheritance confession, counsel, and resurrection-from-Sheol confidence accumulate as one trust testimony.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 5's Yahweh assigned my portion is the strongest positive-confession seam after verses 1-4, but the rejected loyalties define that inheritance claim.

decision_observations.support: The plea of innocence, pursued-speaker complaint, and final rescue request remain addressed to the same judge.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 13's Arise, Yahweh begins the strongest final rescue child, though its adversary and vindication language depends on verses 1-12.

decision_observations.support: The direct lament of 18:1–6 reaches its answer when the temple hears the cry; verse 7's initial Then launches cosmic shaking rather than extending the prayer.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.18.1–50 remains the proper parent arc, but using it alone would erase the heard-cry/then-theophany hinge at 6/7 that makes the opening lament independently intelligible.

decision_observations.support: Verses 7–19 form the rescue theophany: earth, heavens, cloud, thunder, and descent culminate in extraction to a broad place, after which verse 20 begins reward testimony.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Joining 1–19 would preserve crisis and rescue, yet would obscure the explicit Then at 7; extending through 20–30 would cross from narrated divine action into the speaker's account of recompense.

decision_observations.support: The assertion that Yahweh has rewarded the speaker opens a sustained first-person vindication in 18:20–30; the movement closes with confession of God's perfect way before verse 31 begins the warrior recital.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.18.20–45 combines testimony with battle victory, but the divine question at 31 transfers attention from the speaker's righteousness to God's equipping and subduing work.

decision_observations.support: The question about who is God at 18:31 introduces divine equipping, pursuit, and enemy submission through verse 45; the acclamation at 46 converts victory recital into thanksgiving.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Merging 20–45 would conflate the prior reward-for-righteousness testimony with this battle catalogue, despite their different opening formulas and rhetorical aims.

decision_observations.support: The Yahweh-lives acclamation turns 18:46–50 into a royal thanksgiving that names vengeance, deliverance, nations, king, and anointed seed as the poem's close.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The whole Psalm preserves the complete crisis-to-kingship arc, but sole reliance on 1–50 would hide the unmistakable closing doxological turn after the foreigners fade at 45.

decision_observations.support: Heavens, firmament, day, night, and sun sustain creation's wordless witness through 19:6; at verse 7 the subject and lexicon abruptly reset to Yahweh's perfect law.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.19.1–14 is the complete theological poem, but treating it as the only unit would collapse the observable creation, Torah, and prayer progression.

decision_observations.support: The sixfold catalogue of law, testimony, precepts, commandment, fear, and ordinances governs 19:7–11; verse 12 shifts from objective praise to first-person fault discernment.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Combining 1–11 would join creation witness to Torah praise across the verse-7 subject reset; extending past 11 would absorb a personal cleansing prayer into the catalogue it applies.

decision_observations.support: Questions about hidden error open 19:12–14, where cleansing, restraint from presumptuous sin, and acceptable speech form a first-person petition ending in direct address to rock and redeemer.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Whole-Psalm retrieval should remain, but it cannot replace this application movement without losing the pronounced first-person turn after the statutes' warning.

decision_observations.support: Congregational intercession, confidence that the anointed is answered, and a final royal plea enact one compact liturgy.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 6's Now I know changes from wish to assurance, but the confidence explicitly answers the petitions of verses 1-5.

decision_observations.support: Past royal gifts, confidence in steadfast love, future judgment, and final praise trace a single royal thanksgiving.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 7 begins the future-facing trust and judgment movement, yet it grounds that future in the blessings recited in verses 1-6.

decision_observations.support: Forsakenness, remembered trust, mockery, bodily dissolution, encircling enemies, and repeated pleas occupy 22:1–21; the final rescue request is followed at verse 22 by a public vow to proclaim.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.22.1–31 rightly holds lament and answer together, but as the only unit it would conceal the decisive move from unresolved second-person rescue petition to assembly testimony.

challenges.proposed_remedy: The complete arc is retained as parent context; verse 22 begins proclamation among brothers rather than continuing the plea, validating 1–21 as the lament child.
challenges.counterevidence: Ps.22.1–31 rightly holds lament and answer together, but as the only unit it would conceal the decisive move from unresolved second-person rescue petition to assembly testimony.

decision_observations.support: At 22:22 the speaker promises public naming among brothers; assembly praise then widens to nations and unborn generations through verse 31.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Merging back to verse 1 would preserve the lament-to-praise arc but would make the post-rescue assembly hymn less retrievable and blur its expanding audiences.

decision_observations.support: Shepherd care through danger, host hospitality, and lifelong dwelling are linked metaphors of one trust confession.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 5's table image is the strongest metaphor shift, but it intensifies rather than replaces the guidance and protection of verses 1-4.

decision_observations.support: The earth, its fullness, the world, seas, and floods make 24:1–2 a compact creator-kingship proclamation; the ascent question at verse 3 opens a liturgical interrogation.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.24.1–10 preserves creator and entering king together, but it does not nullify the form change from declarative cosmic ownership to question-and-answer entrance speech.

decision_observations.support: The ascent question in 24:3 receives its qualifications—clean hands, pure heart, truthful worship—and resolves with the seeking generation at verse 6; verse 7 then addresses gates directly.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.24.1–6 would keep creator sovereignty with admission requirements, but crosses from proclamation into a self-contained question-and-answer rite at verse 3.

decision_observations.support: Repeated commands for gates to lift their heads and alternating questions and answers about the King of glory organize 24:7–10 as a gate antiphony.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The complete Psalm remains the larger entrance composition, yet merging 7–10 into it would erase the repeated antiphonal script that begins only after the seeker saying.

decision_observations.support: The alphabetic lament interweaves guidance petition, instruction about Yahweh's ways, and renewed distress without completing a child before its final redemption plea.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 8 could open a teaching child and verse 16 a renewed personal lament, but the alphabetic sequence and repeated way language bind all three movements.

decision_observations.support: Vindication plea, separation from evildoers, altar procession, and final congregational blessing enact one integrity prayer.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 6's hand-washing and altar approach is the strongest cultic turn, but it demonstrates the integrity claimed in verses 1-5 and supports the rescue plea in verses 9-12.

decision_observations.support: Fearless confidence, temple desire, urgent Hear petition, and final waiting exhortation create a trust-lament-trust arc.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 7's renewed direct plea is the material 1-6/7-14 alternative; the final Wait for Yahweh deliberately returns to the opening confidence.

decision_observations.support: The opening rescue plea and warning about evildoers turn into thanksgiving and a communal shepherd blessing.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 6's Blessed be Yahweh is a real lament-to-thanks seam, but verses 8-9 extend the speaker's heard prayer to the people rather than forming a detached hymn.

decision_observations.support: The heavenly summons, sevenfold voice over the storm, and enthroned peace blessing form a single divine-kingship hymn.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 3 begins the storm theophany after the summons, while verse 10 interprets it as kingship; neither movement closes independently of the other two.

decision_observations.support: Rescue thanksgiving, recalled self-confidence and distress, then mourning-to-dancing praise narrate one reversal testimony.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 6 begins the crisis recollection and verse 11 returns to praise; the framing thanksgiving makes those shifts a single narrated deliverance.

decision_observations.support: Refuge appeals, entrusted spirit, rejection of idols, and the testimony of feet set in a broad place shape 31:1–8; verse 9's fresh mercy plea reopens distress.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The whole Psalm is a continuous refuge prayer, but using 1–24 alone would conceal the movement from initial confidence to renewed bodily and social anguish at verse 9.

decision_observations.support: From the mercy plea in 31:9, failing strength, reproach, isolation, plots, and enemy shame carry the renewed lament through verse 18; verse 19 turns to stored goodness.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.31.1–18 would combine two petition cycles, but the delivered-feet closure at 8 and new bodily complaint at 9 prevent that merger from being the sharper retrieval span.

decision_observations.support: The goodness exclamation begins 31:19–24, moving from complaint to protected presence, testimony of answered prayer, and exhortation for the faithful to love and be strong.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Whole-Psalm treatment safeguards the complete trust journey, but would underdescribe the public praise-and-exhortation form that follows the silencing of lying lips.

decision_observations.support: Forgiveness beatitudes, concealed-and-confessed sin, then instruction and communal rejoicing build one penitential wisdom testimony.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The Selah after verse 5 marks the strongest confession-to-instruction alternative, but verses 6-11 apply the forgiveness learned in verses 1-5.

decision_observations.support: Praise summons, creation by Yahweh's word, sovereignty over nations, and waiting trust all support one hymn of reliable counsel.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 10 begins the nations-and-counsel contrast and verse 18 the trust conclusion; both depend on the creator-word praise of verses 4-9.

decision_observations.support: The personal praise and deliverance testimony become communal instruction at Come, you children and end with refuge.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 11 is the actual testimony-to-wisdom seam, yet the instruction generalizes the tasted deliverance of verses 1-10 within one alphabetic poem.

decision_observations.support: In 35:1–10 the speaker asks Yahweh to contend and pursue, imagines enemy collapse, then vows whole-being praise; verse 11 introduces false witnesses as a new accusation.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.35.1–28 is one adversary lament, but sole whole-Psalm retrieval would hide the first petition-and-praise-vow cycle before the legal-witness complaint begins.

decision_observations.support: False witnesses open 35:11–18; the speaker contrasts their harm with his mourning conduct and ends by promising assembly praise, before verse 19 renews petition.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Joining 1–18 would combine two accusation cycles despite the first praise vow at 10 and the new witness charge at 11; extending beyond 18 would cross another completed vow.

decision_observations.support: The renewed prohibition against enemy rejoicing opens 35:19–28, where requests for exposure and vindication culminate in continual praise.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The full lament remains the parent, yet merging 19–28 backward would ignore the assembly vow at 18 and the fresh imperatival petition at 19.

decision_observations.support: The oracle about wickedness gives way to direct praise of Yahweh's steadfast love and then a preservation petition.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 5 is the material wickedness-oracle to hymn seam corroborated by a WEB paragraph; the closing petition applies that hymn to the opening threat.

decision_observations.support: Fret-not commands, trust, waiting, and meek inheritance give 37:1–11 a discernible opening exhortation, but verse 12's wicked plotting continues the same alphabetic righteous-and-wicked pedagogy.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Keeping only Ps.37.1–40 would honor the continuous wisdom acrostic; splitting at 11/12 would improve topical retrieval but may overstate a shift inside an uninterrupted alternation.

decision_observations.support: Plotting, divine laughter, weapons, and the opposed futures of wicked and righteous cluster in 37:12–20, although verse 21's borrower-and-giver contrast continues the same moral sequence.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.37.1–20 joins exhortation and fate contrast under one sustained acrostic discourse; the 11/12 topical turn may justify a child, but not with enough force to defeat the larger option conclusively.

decision_observations.support: Borrowing and generosity lead through ordered steps, durable inheritance, and Torah in the heart across 37:21–31; wicked watching at 32 changes topic without changing wisdom form.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.37.21–40 could encompass the righteous path and closing threat-and-refuge contrast; the proposed 31/32 seam is topical rather than a decisive formal break.

decision_observations.support: Wicked surveillance, waiting for Yahweh, observed transgressors, and final refuge shape 37:32–40 as a closing counsel, though it remains inseparable in form from the preceding acrostic wisdom.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The whole 1–40 Psalm is the strongest formal unit; a 32–40 child gains a closing conflict-and-refuge focus but risks mistaking topical concentration for stanza closure.

decision_observations.support: Wrath, bodily collapse, isolation, enemies, confession, and final Hurry to help me remain one unrelieved penitential address.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 15's For in you, Yahweh, do I hope is the strongest confidence turn, but it immediately returns to the same pain, sin, and adversaries.

decision_observations.support: A vow of silence breaks into a mortality prayer and then a hope-and-forgiveness petition.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 7's Now, Lord, what do I wait for? is the strongest mortality-to-hope seam, while the failed silence and brevity of life govern the closing appeal.

decision_observations.support: Pit rescue, new song, opened ears, willing obedience, and public declaration form the thanksgiving testimony of 40:1–10; the request not to withhold tender mercies at 11 resumes supplication.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.40.1–17 preserves thanksgiving framed by distress, but as the sole span it would blur the completed public testimony before the later danger petition.

decision_observations.support: At 40:11 the speaker again petitions for mercy amid surrounding evils, hostile wishes, poverty, and need for swift help through verse 17.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Merging 11–17 into the whole Psalm honors its framed composition, but loses the shift from retrospective public witness to present first-person emergency.

decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.44.1–26 is the complete communal argument, but sole use of it would flatten the deliberate contrast between remembered victory and current rejection.

decision_observations.support: Rejection, retreat, plunder, scattering, reproach, and taunt define 44:9–16; verse 17's summary of what has befallen the people begins an innocence protest rather than another defeat detail.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Joining 1–16 would preserve memory-versus-defeat contrast, yet would absorb the explicit reversal at verse 9; extending past 16 would cross into the covenant-loyalty defense.

decision_observations.support: The acknowledgment of all that has come upon the people opens 44:17–26, where the community asserts covenant loyalty and turns that claim into wake-and-rescue petitions grounded in loving kindness.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The complete Psalm better displays the paradox of faithful suffering, but cannot replace the final defense without obscuring its shift from reported defeat to innocence-based appeal.

decision_observations.support: God-as-refuge holds 46:1–3 together while earth moves, mountains fall, and waters roar; the scene resolves at Selah before verse 4 introduces the city's river.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.46.1–11 is a refrain-bound hymn and must remain the parent, yet exposing only it would conceal the first catastrophe-and-refuge strophe.

decision_observations.support: River, holy city, divine presence, shaking nations, and the Yahweh-of-Armies refrain form 46:4–7; the invitation to come and see at verse 8 opens a new summons.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.46.1–7 would combine danger and Zion stability, but crosses the shift from chaotic waters to the life-giving river; the complete Psalm remains the parent.

decision_observations.support: The invitation to inspect Yahweh's works initiates 46:8–11: ended wars, broken weapons, stillness, universal exaltation, and the returning refrain constitute the final kingship-oracle cycle.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Whole-Psalm retrieval preserves the triple-strophe hymn; it does not erase the direct invitation at 8 following a completed refrain.

decision_observations.support: Nations are summoned, Yahweh ascends amid acclamation, and the rulers gather under divine kingship.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The Selah after verse 4 marks a plausible 1-4/5-9 turn from summons to ascent, but the repeated kingship praise joins both movements.

decision_observations.support: Zion praise, failed royal assault, temple meditation, and processional inspection culminate in this God is our God.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 9's temple meditation after the assault is the strongest historical-to-processional seam, though the inspected city is the same Zion praised and defended earlier.

decision_observations.support: A universal command to hear culminates in proverb, riddle, and harp at 49:1–4; verse 5's fear question starts the mortality reasoning.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.49.1–20 is one wisdom discourse, but retaining only it would hide the conventional audience summons before the speaker begins his argument.

decision_observations.support: The fear question in 49:5 unfolds through ransom's limits, grave inevitability, and honor without understanding to the mortality comparison at verse 12; verse 13 resumes as a warning about destiny.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.49.1–12 would attach the summons to its first argument, but the proverb introduction ends at 4; merging 5–20 would weaken the refrain-like restatement at 12/13.

decision_observations.support: The destiny formula reopens the warning at 49:13; self-confident wealth, grave shepherding, divine redemption, and the repeated human-beast comparison run through verse 20.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The entire Psalm preserves one meditation, yet merging 13–20 backward would blur the deliberate restart after the first mortality refrain.

decision_observations.support: Divine appearing, fire, gathered covenant people, and witnessing heavens stage a courtroom summons in 50:1–6; direct address to the people at verse 7 begins adjudication.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.50.1–23 is the complete courtroom speech, but as the only span it would merge the narrated convening of court with the oracle delivered inside it.

decision_observations.support: Direct address to the people opens 50:7–15, correcting sacrifice assumptions through divine ownership, thanksgiving, vows, and the call-in-trouble promise; verse 16 redirects speech to the wicked.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.50.1–15 would combine court summons and first oracle, but crosses the direct-address onset at 7; carrying beyond 15 would ignore an explicit addressee change.

decision_observations.support: The address to the wicked begins 50:16–23, indicting hypocritical statute-recitation through theft, adultery, and slander before warning and promising salvation to ordered conduct.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The complete Psalm preserves one judgment event, but exclusive whole-unit retrieval would suppress the direct transfer from worship instruction to the wicked's ethical indictment.

decision_observations.support: Transgression, inherited guilt, and inward truth sustain 51:1–6 as confession and cleansing plea; verse 7's purification request begins the concrete restoration sequence, with WEB coordinates understood through the two-verse MT title offset.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.51.1–19 is the primary penitential prayer, but using it alone would obscure the movement from acknowledgment of guilt to requested purification.

decision_observations.support: Hyssop, washing, restored joy, clean heart, and renewed spirit organize 51:7–12; verse 13's prospective teaching vow changes the restored speaker from petitioner to witness.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.51.1–12 joins confession and renewal, but crosses the shift at verse 7; extending into verse 13 would absorb the resulting teaching vow into the restoration request.

decision_observations.support: The teaching promise initiates 51:13–19, moving through converted sinners, praising lips, contrite sacrifice, and a final prayer for Zion.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Whole-Psalm retrieval safeguards the prayer's full logic, yet cannot replace the post-renewal vow without hiding its changed outward purpose and closing communal horizon.

decision_observations.support: The denunciation of the boastful speaker, the righteous community's response, and the olive-tree trust confession form a single contrast psalm.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 6 could begin the righteous observers' response and verse 8 the personal trust close, but both derive their force from the accusation in verses 1-5.

decision_observations.support: The fool-and-corruption portrait, divine inspection and fear, then the Zion salvation wish compress a complete wisdom lament.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 6's salvation prayer is the strongest close, but it answers the universal corruption of verses 1-5 rather than opening a new poem.

decision_observations.support: A rescue plea, confidence that God is helper, and a freewill-offering vow narrate one short deliverance arc.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 4's Behold, God is my helper is a real petition-to-confidence turn, but verses 6-7 explicitly fulfill the opening request.

decision_observations.support: Attentive prayer, restless anguish, betrayal, fear, and the wish for dove-like escape fill 55:1–8; the confusion petition at verse 9 redirects lament toward city violence.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.55.1–23 is one betrayal lament, but exclusive use of the whole would hide the move from personal flight fantasy to a petition about the city's speech and oppression.

decision_observations.support: The petition to confuse speech leads 55:9–15 through city violence, intimate companionship, and a death wish; the speaker's self-contrast at verse 16 turns from accusation to trust.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.55.1–15 would unite fear and betrayal complaint, but crosses the spatial and rhetorical reset at verse 9; carrying beyond 15 would ignore the personal trust contrast.

decision_observations.support: The speaker's declaration that he will call on God opens 55:16–23, where regular prayer, confidence in being heard, betrayal reflection, burden-casting exhortation, and trust conclude the Psalm.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The full poem keeps betrayal and trust together, but sole parent retrieval would understate the direct contrast and practical exhortation that begin after the death wish.

decision_observations.support: Fear, hostile surveillance, tear-counting, repeated trust, and thanksgiving vows recur around the same persecution.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 8's request to record wandering is the strongest renewed-trust movement, yet the repeated I will not be afraid refrain binds both halves.

decision_observations.support: Mercy, refuge beneath wings, hostile trampling, and the plea for divine exaltation compose 57:1–5; after the refrain, verse 6 reports the enemies' trap reversing on them.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.57.1–11 is a deliberately refrain-framed whole, yet exposing only it would conceal the first refuge plea before reversal and awakened praise.

decision_observations.support: The enemies' net becomes their own fall in 57:6, leading to a steadfast heart, awakened instruments, nations praise, and the returning exaltation refrain through verse 11.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Merging 6–11 into the whole preserves plea and answer, but would make the reversal-and-praise half less directly retrievable despite its separate refrain frame.

decision_observations.support: Indictment of unjust rulers, imprecatory images, and the righteous conclusion form one judicial imprecation.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 6 begins the judgment petition and verse 10 the observer response; separating them would detach verdict and consequence from the indictment.

decision_observations.support: Rescue pleas, prowling enemies, divine laughter, and the speaker's watch upon divine strength run through 59:1–9, but the strength-and-watch language continues into verse 10 rather than yielding an uncontested seam.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.59.1–17 may be the only stable unit; alternatively, recurrent dog, Selah, and strength patterns may favor 1–5, 6–13, and 14–17 instead of the current 1–9 and 10–17 division.

decision_observations.support: Anticipated mercy, petitions about enemy scattering, returning dogs, morning song, and high-tower praise occupy 59:10–17, but strength, watch, and prowling motifs cross the proposed 9/10 edge.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The received Psalm may be the only secure unit; if children are required, the recurring dog, Selah, and strength pattern plausibly favors 1–5, 6–13, and 14–17 over 1–9 and 10–17.

decision_observations.support: Defeat lament, territorial divine oracle, and military petition stage one communal crisis.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The Selah after verse 4 and oracle opening at verse 6 support a real 1-5/6-12 alternative, but the oracle does not resolve the final Who will lead us? petition.

decision_observations.support: Remote-ground plea, refuge confidence, royal preservation prayer, and perpetual praise vow remain one royal lament.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 5's For you, God, have heard my vows begins the royal-confidence movement, but it answers the opening cry and leads directly to the closing vow.

decision_observations.support: Silent waiting, rock-and-salvation trust, attackers, and Selah shape 62:1–4; verse 5 repeats the trust language as direct self-address, making a plausible but not compulsory new movement.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.62.1–12 is formally unified by recurring trust language; a three-child reading gains support from self-address and the later wealth warning, while Selah alone cannot authorize it.

challenges.claim: Ps.62.1–12 is formally unified by recurring trust language; a three-child reading gains support from self-address and the later wealth warning, while Selah alone cannot authorize it.

challenges.counterevidence: Ps.62.1–12 is formally unified by recurring trust language; a three-child reading gains support from self-address and the later wealth warning, while Selah alone cannot authorize it.

decision_observations.support: Renewed self-address, repeated rock imagery, and public trust exhortation fill 62:5–8; verse 9 changes from trusting God to evaluating social rank and riches.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.62.1–8 would preserve the doubled trust refrain, while the current child highlights its second, exhortative presentation; neither Selah nor repetition alone settles the choice.

challenges.counterevidence: Ps.62.1–8 would preserve the doubled trust refrain, while the current child highlights its second, exhortative presentation; neither Selah nor repetition alone settles the choice.

decision_observations.support: Low and high people, extortion, riches, once-and-twice-heard power, loving kindness, and recompense give 62:9–12 a compact wisdom oracle after the public trust call.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The whole Psalm preserves the relation between trust and false securities, but sole use of it would obscure the direct social and wealth warning begun at verse 9.

decision_observations.support: Thirst for God, remembered sanctuary praise, satisfied meditation, and enemies' fate form a single trust testimony.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 5's satisfaction image is the strongest longing-to-fulfillment seam, while the remembered praise and refuge under wings bridge the two movements.

decision_observations.support: Secret-plot complaint is answered by sudden divine shooting and communal fear and rejoicing.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 7's But God will shoot at them is the real complaint-to-reversal turn; the reversal is unintelligible without the speech-weapons of verses 1-6.

decision_observations.support: Atonement and temple blessedness, cosmic stilling, and harvest abundance develop one thanksgiving-creation hymn.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 9's turn to watered earth is the strongest cosmic-to-harvest seam; the creator who stills seas in verses 5-8 is the same giver of the harvest.

decision_observations.support: Universal summons and exodus testing widen into a first-person vow and answered-prayer testimony.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 13's I will come into your temple with burnt offerings is the material communal-to-personal seam, but the individual testimony exemplifies the communal call rather than replacing it.

decision_observations.support: A priestly blessing petition widens through knowledge among nations to the peoples-praise line at 67:3; verse 4 may begin a central strophe, but the repeated praise line can also bind 1–5.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.67.1–7 is the stable hymn, and 1–5 is a live alternative because verses 3 and 5 frame one nations-praise complex rather than necessarily closing separate strophes.

challenges.claim: Ps.67.1–7 is the stable hymn, and 1–5 is a live alternative because verses 3 and 5 frame one nations-praise complex rather than necessarily closing separate strophes.

challenges.counterevidence: Ps.67.1–7 is the stable hymn, and 1–5 is a live alternative because verses 3 and 5 frame one nations-praise complex rather than necessarily closing separate strophes.

decision_observations.support: Glad nations, equitable judgment, guided peoples, and renewed praise make 67:4–5 a compact center; whether verse 3 closes the prior strophe or opens a refrain frame remains disputed.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.67.1–5 plausibly binds blessing and nations praise between repeated lines; isolating 4–5 gives sharper function but depends on one interpretation of the refrain.

challenges.claim: Ps.67.1–5 plausibly binds blessing and nations praise between repeated lines; isolating 4–5 gives sharper function but depends on one interpretation of the refrain.

challenges.counterevidence: Ps.67.1–5 plausibly binds blessing and nations praise between repeated lines; isolating 4–5 gives sharper function but depends on one interpretation of the refrain.

decision_observations.support: Earth yielding produce and repeated divine blessing form the harvest consequence in 67:6–7 after the final peoples-praise line.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Whole-Psalm retrieval preserves blessing, mission, praise, and harvest together, yet cannot replace the clear result movement introduced by the earth's yield.

decision_observations.support: Rising-God acclamation, fleeing enemies, care for the fatherless and lonely, families, and released prisoners organize 68:1–6; verse 7's remembered departure begins historical march recital.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.68.1–35 remains the complex processional parent, but treating it as indivisible would hide the shift from summons and divine character to narrated Exodus-Sinai action.

decision_observations.support: The remembered departure carries 68:7–18 from Sinai through rain, hosts, Bashan, chariots, and ascent; the blessing at verse 19 starts fresh daily-bearing praise.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.68.1–18 would attach the summons to its historical grounding, but crosses the narrative onset at 7; extending past 18 would absorb a new acclamation after the ascent.

decision_observations.support: The blessing of the Lord who daily bears burdens opens 68:19–27, joining salvation, defeated enemies, procession, singers, musicians, and named tribes; verse 28 begins an appeal for commanded strength.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.68.19–35 could unite procession and kingdom praise, but would flatten the shift from describing the procession to petitioning God and addressing kingdoms.

decision_observations.support: Commanded strength, temple gifts, rebuked beasts, incoming kingdoms, and rider-of-heavens praise make 68:28–35 the kingdom doxology.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The complete Psalm is indispensable context, but exclusive parent retrieval would obscure the closing international appeal and cosmic praise that follow the named procession.

decision_observations.support: Flood depth, mire, exhausted crying, hatred without cause, and alienation from kin and gate-sitters sustain 69:1–12; the speaker's self-contrast at 13 redirects complaint into rescue petition.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.69.1–36 is one lament-to-praise composition, but as the only unit it would hide the explicit self-contrast after the opening catalogue of distress.

decision_observations.support: At the acceptable time, 69:13–18 asks for loving kindness, answered prayer, firm footing, and rescue from waters and enemies; verse 19 turns to known reproach and its offenders.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.69.1–18 would keep distress and rescue plea together, but crosses the speaker's self-contrast at 13; extending into 19–28 would merge petition for self with imprecation against adversaries.

decision_observations.support: Known reproach, broken heart, absent comforters, gall and vinegar, and escalating judgments against enemies dominate 69:19–28; verse 29's return to the speaker's pain turns toward praise and Zion hope.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.69.19–36 would join imprecation and eventual thanksgiving, but would blur the reversal from enemy-directed curses to the afflicted speaker's sung praise.

decision_observations.support: The speaker's renewed statement of pain opens 69:29–36, where anticipated salvation becomes song, afflicted encouragement, cosmic praise, and restored Zion.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Whole-Psalm retrieval preserves the complete descent-to-restoration trajectory, but cannot replace the final thanksgiving and communal hope without losing its changed horizon.

decision_observations.support: Petition against persecutors, blessing for seekers, and the poor speaker's closing urgency form one intentionally brief lament.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 4's turn to seekers is the only plausible inner seam, but it is a one-verse counterwish between the adversary petition and personal plea.

decision_observations.support: Lifelong refuge, dependence from birth, aged weakness, accusers, and pleas not to be forsaken organize 71:1–13; verse 14's declaration of continuing hope begins a vow of praise and teaching.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.71.1–24 is the natural lifelong-trust prayer, yet sole use of it would hide the deliberate movement from danger petition to future witness.

decision_observations.support: Continual hope in 71:14 expands into proclaimed righteousness, remembered teaching, old-age witness, divine acts, music, and rejoicing lips through verse 24.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Merging 14–24 into the complete prayer preserves the life-course arc, but makes the post-petition teaching and praise vow less directly retrievable.

decision_observations.support: The royal justice prayer expands to worldwide blessing, followed by a doxology and editorial colophon.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 18 begins the collection doxology and verse 20 the colophon; their retrieval treatment remains a coda-policy hold while the WEB Psalm stays whole.

decision_observations.support: The speaker's admitted envy introduces 73:1–12, a sustained portrayal of the wicked's ease, pride, violence, mockery, and apparent prosperity; verse 13 turns inward to the cost of purity.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.73.1–28 is one crisis-to-nearness argument, but exclusive whole-unit retrieval would flatten its observation, personal crisis, reappraisal, and confession stages.

decision_observations.support: The claim of having cleansed the heart in vain begins 73:13–17; the speaker's crisis becomes unspeakable until sanctuary entry changes his understanding.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.73.1–17 could unite observed prosperity and the resulting crisis, but crosses the inward turn at 13; extending past 17 would absorb the fate disclosed by sanctuary insight.

decision_observations.support: Sanctuary insight yields 73:18–22: slippery places, sudden desolation, dreamlike disappearance, and the speaker's beastlike self-rebuke reverse his former estimate; the adversative at 23 turns to abiding nearness.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.73.18–28 could join reappraisal and confession, but would weaken the explicit adversative that moves from brutishness to continual divine grasp.

decision_observations.support: The continuing-nearness confession begins 73:23–28, joining divine grasp, counsel, heavenly desire, failing flesh, nearness, and public testimony.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The complete Psalm best conveys transformation, yet using it alone would obscure the final confession's direct contrast with the beastlike self-assessment at verse 22.

decision_observations.support: Abandoned sanctuary, enemy roar, burned meeting places, absent signs, and the question of the withheld hand fill 74:1–11; the kingship confession at 12 turns from ruin to creation memory.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.74.1–23 holds complaint, memory, and covenant plea together, but sole parent retrieval would erase the sharp affirmation that interrupts the destruction lament.

decision_observations.support: The kingship confession introduces 74:12–17, recalling divided sea, crushed monsters, springs, day, night, sun, seasons, and earth's boundaries; verse 18 returns with an imperative to remember present reproach.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.74.1–17 would join crisis and theological counter-memory, but crosses the verse-12 affirmation; extending into 18–23 would merge recital with covenant petition.

decision_observations.support: The remembrance imperative opens 74:18–23, where reproach, the vulnerable dove, covenant darkness, the poor person's cause, and pleas to arise close the Psalm.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Whole-Psalm retrieval preserves the entire lament, yet would underdescribe the final covenant-based petition after the cosmic recital.

decision_observations.support: Opening thanks introduces divine speech about appointed judgment, human interpretation, and a closing vow.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 2 begins the judgment oracle and verse 9 the speaker's vow; the answer to arrogant boasting needs both voice movements.

decision_observations.support: Zion victory praise, terrifying judgment from heaven, and a final vow exhortation describe one divine-warrior hymn.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 10 opens the strongest judgment-to-vow application, but it is the human response demanded by the victory of verses 1-9.

decision_observations.support: Night crying, refused comfort, remembered song, and six questions about vanished favor sustain 77:1–9; the deliberate appeal at verse 10 redirects doubt into chosen remembrance.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.77.1–20 is the complete lament-to-theophany arc, but exclusive whole-unit retrieval would hide the stated cognitive turn after the grace question.

decision_observations.support: The deliberate appeal begins 77:10–15, where former years, deeds, wonders, holiness, redemption, and Jacob become the chosen answer to doubt; verse 16 makes the waters themselves react.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.77.1–15 would combine anguished questions with their memory response, but crosses the explicit cognitive turn at 10; extending beyond 15 would merge reflection with narrated theophany.

decision_observations.support: Waters seeing God opens 77:16–20; trembling depths, pouring clouds, thunder, lightning, earthquake, sea-path, unseen footprints, and shepherded people complete the Exodus theophany.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The whole Psalm preserves the movement from sleepless lament to saving memory, yet exclusive use of it would make the final water-theophany less directly retrievable.

decision_observations.support: Commands to listen, explicit parable-and-riddle language, transmitted testimony, and warning about the fathers establish 78:1–8 as the teaching prologue; verse 9 begins the first named episode with Ephraim.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.78.1–72 is the governing historical instruction, but as the only span it would hide the poem's stated pedagogical program before the narrative examples.

decision_observations.support: Ephraim's retreat in 78:9 contrasts with covenant wonders, divided sea, cloud, fire, rock, and supplied water through verse 16; renewed sin at 17 restarts rebellion.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.78.1–16 could attach the prologue to its first example, but crosses the named-episode onset at 9; extending farther would absorb a new sin-and-judgment cycle.

decision_observations.support: Renewed sin starts 78:17–31, tracing craving, table-testing, unbelief, manna, meat, and wrath to judgment; verse 32 resumes the rebellion despite all this.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.78.17–39 would combine two rebellion cycles, but would mute the completed craving-and-wrath episode before the resumptive formula at 32.

decision_observations.support: The confession that sin persisted despite prior judgment opens 78:32–39, where unbelief, shortened days, superficial return, remembered Rock, flattering mouths, and divine compassion complete a second cycle.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Joining 17–39 would preserve repeated rebellion as one movement; the current child is preferable for retrieval because verse 32 deliberately resumes after judgment and verse 40 changes to retrospective recital.

decision_observations.support: The retrospective question at 78:40 introduces wilderness provocation, Egypt's plagues, sea crossing, guidance, conquest, and land gift through verse 55; verse 56 reverses the gift with renewed testing.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.78.40–64 could unite deliverance and subsequent Shiloh defeat, but would obscure the adversative contrast after the land has been given.

decision_observations.support: Renewed testing opens 78:56–64, linking deceitful-bow rebellion, high places, Shiloh abandonment, captivity, and priestly loss; verse 65's awakening simile begins restoration and election.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.78.40–64 would place deliverance and failure together, but crosses the verse-56 reversal; extending beyond 64 would merge defeat with the Lord's renewed action.

decision_observations.support: The Lord's awakening starts 78:65–72, moving through defeated foes, rejection of Joseph, choice of Judah and Zion, and David's skillful shepherding as the historical poem's closure.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The whole Psalm preserves the complete teaching history, but sole parent retrieval would hide the final election resolution after Shiloh's defeat.

decision_observations.support: Temple devastation and national reproach become confession, mercy plea, and promised thanks.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 5's How long? is the strongest description-to-petition seam, while the plea repeatedly names the devastation and reproach it seeks to reverse.

decision_observations.support: Shepherd invocation, enthroned glory, tribal appeal, and the restoration plea carry 80:1–3 to the first refrain; verse 4 renews complaint after that formal closure.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.80.1–19 is strongly unified by the threefold restoration refrain, yet exposing only the whole would conceal the refrain-bounded opening invocation.

decision_observations.support: The how-long question opens 80:4–7, describing anger, tears, neighbor strife, and enemy laughter before the restoration refrain returns; verse 8 then introduces the vine from Egypt.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.80.1–7 would join invocation and complaint across the first refrain, but the repeated close at 3 and fresh complaint at 4 argue against that merger as the primary child.

decision_observations.support: The vine brought from Egypt begins 80:8–19; planting, broken walls, ravaging beasts, divine visitation, chosen son, revived people, and the expanded refrain sustain the final plea.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The complete Psalm remains the refrain-bound parent, but would underdescribe the long vine allegory and its final restoration request if used alone.

decision_observations.support: Joyful song, instruments, trumpet, appointed feast, statute, and Joseph testimony shape the festival summons of 81:1–5; verse 6 changes to first-person divine recollection of released burdens.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.81.1–16 is the complete festival-and-oracle composition, but exclusive whole-unit retrieval would blur the shift from communal summons to divine speech.

decision_observations.support: The first-person oracle in 81:6–10 recalls released burdens, hidden thunder, Meribah, exclusive worship, and the open-mouth promise; the people's refusal at 11 turns promise into lament and conditional consequence.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.81.1–10 would unite festival setting with the first oracle, but crosses the speaker change at 6; continuing beyond 10 would absorb the explicit refusal reversal.

decision_observations.support: The people's refusal opens 81:11–16, moving from stubborn walking to the unrealized defeat of enemies and promised wheat and honey.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The complete Psalm best displays summons, command, refusal, and lost abundance, yet cannot replace the final conditional lament without hiding its explicit reversal.

decision_observations.support: The divine-council setting, indictment of unjust judges, death verdict, and final appeal form one judicial oracle.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 2 begins the accusation and verse 8 the appeal, but removing either would leave the council scene without charge or requested enforcement.

decision_observations.support: A plea against divine silence leads 83:1–8 through conspiracy, intent to erase Israel, and an enumerated coalition; verse 9's comparative petition converts the list into historical analogy and requested action.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.83.1–18 is the complete conspiracy lament, but as the only span it would conceal the passage's move from identifying the coalition to requesting analogous judgment.

decision_observations.support: The historical comparison begins 83:9–18, invoking Midian, Sisera, Oreb, and Zebah before escalating through whirlwind, fire, shame, and the hope that enemies seek Yahweh's name.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Merging the section into the whole preserves crisis and response, but would make the historical-analogy and judgment petition less directly retrievable after the nation list ends.

decision_observations.support: Longing for Yahweh's courts, pilgrimage beatitudes, an anointed-one prayer, and the final trust beatitude form one Zion song.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 5 begins the pilgrimage movement and verse 9 the direct prayer; repeated blessedness language binds them to the opening longing.

decision_observations.support: Remembered restoration leads to renewed mercy petition and then a heard oracle of peace, love, and righteousness.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 8's I will hear what God, Yahweh, will speak is the strongest petition-to-oracle seam, but the oracle answers the restoration plea of verses 4-7.

decision_observations.support: Personal plea, incomparable-God hymn, request for an undivided heart, and enemy complaint remain one sustained address.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 8 could open the hymn and verse 11 the teaching petition, but the speaker uses both to ground the same rescue request.

decision_observations.support: Yahweh's love of Zion, enrollment of foreign nations, and the singers' closing claim create one compact Zion oracle.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 4 begins the nations list, but the list is the content of Zion's glorious report rather than an independent register.

decision_observations.support: Opening cry, descent-to-Sheol imagery, questions about praise among the dead, and final darkness never reach a confidence resolution.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Verse 10 begins the strongest rhetorical-question movement and verse 13 renews direct prayer, but the uninterrupted abandonment argues for the whole lament.

decision_observations.support: A vow to sing enduring loving kindness frames 89:1–4, including the reported promise of Davidic offspring and throne; verse 5 turns from the vow and promise to heavenly praise.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.89.1–52 is the governing covenant hymn and lament, but sole whole-unit retrieval would hide the concise programmatic vow before the cosmic hymn begins.

challenges.counterevidence: Ps.89.1–52 is the governing covenant hymn and lament, but sole whole-unit retrieval would hide the concise programmatic vow before the cosmic hymn begins.

decision_observations.support: Heavenly praise, incomparable divine rule, crushed Rahab, created north and south, righteousness, and the blessed people sustain 89:5–18; the vision formula at 19 begins a Davidic oracle.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.89.1–18 would join the opening covenant vow with cosmic praise, but crosses the verse-5 scenic change; extending farther would merge hymn with vision speech.

decision_observations.support: The vision formula opens 89:19–37, appointing David, promising strength and lineage, describing discipline, and swearing enduring covenant fidelity; the rejection statement at 38 reverses the oracle into lament.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.89.19–45 would keep promise and apparent contradiction together, but would collapse an explicitly reported covenant oracle into the royal rejection that disputes it.

decision_observations.support: The rejection statement begins 89:38–45, reversing covenant assurances with profaned crown, broken walls, plunder, shortened youth, and shame; verse 46 opens the delay question.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.89.19–45 captures promise and rejection together, yet would hide the formal adversative at 38 and prevent direct retrieval of the contradiction movement.

decision_observations.support: The delay question at 89:46 opens a three-verse mortality plea: hidden wrath, life's brevity, and the question of who can escape Sheol run through verse 48; verse 49 begins a different covenant-memory complaint.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.89.46–52 is not one local movement: verses 46–48 address delay and mortality, verses 49–51 ask about former loving kindness and servant reproach, and verse 52 supplies the collection doxology.

decision_observations.support: Verses 49–51 ask where the former loving kindness has gone and bring servant reproach and the enemies' taunt before Yahweh; verse 52 then supplies the collection blessing with its doubled Amen. decision_observations.support: Verses 1–6 move from the confession that the Lord has been Israel's dwelling through divine eternity to the human return to dust, then linger on sleep and morning grass as images of transience. decision_observations.support: The repeated anger language, exposed iniquities, and days passing under wrath bind 90:7–11; verse 12 converts that diagnosis into the imperative petition teach us to number our days and its goal, a heart of wisdom. decision_observations.support: The command Consider in 94:8 introduces a compact rebuttal: the maker of the ear hears, the former of the eye sees, the instructor of nations corrects, and Yahweh knows human thoughts. decision_observations.support: Ps.104.1–9 praises the creator's cosmic architecture—light as clothing, heavens as tent, cloud chariot, winds as messengers, earth founded, waters fleeing and assigned a boundary. decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.104.1–35 remains the encompassing creation hymn, but it cannot replace a locator for the primordial ordering scene. decision_observations.support: Beginning with springs in valleys, 104:10–18 traces provision through animal drink, bird dwellings, rain-fed hills, grass and crops, wine, oil and bread, nourished trees, and mountain refuges. decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.104.1–18 would couple cosmic ordering with the habitats it enables, a valid larger sequence, but it erases the 9/10 change from restraining waters to distributing them for life. decision_observations.support: The moon's appointed seasons and the sun's setting introduce a compact alternation: darkness releases forest animals and lions, sunrise gathers them to dens, and the human worker then goes out until evening. decision_observations.support: Yahweh, how many are your works! at 104:24 opens a panoramic creature inventory, moving to the sea, ships and Leviathan, then to all creatures waiting for food. decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.104.19–30 would present time and creature dependence together, but the new exclamation at 24 and the sea-wide expansion make a real rhetorical restart. Moon/sun scheduling in 19–23 is a finished vignette; 24–30 asks how the multitude exists moment by moment from divine provision and breath.

decision_observations.support: After creation is renewed in 104:30, verses 31–35 turn explicitly to response: may Yahweh's glory endure, may he rejoice in his works, and the singer will praise throughout life. decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.107.10–22 would combine prisoners and the sick because both suffer through rebellion, yet each has its own plight, cry, mode of rescue, and thanksgiving close. The prisoner doors and bars reach closure at 16; illness and loathed food are a new exemplum.

decision_observations.support: Fools are afflicted because of their disobedience opens the third case: they abhor food and approach death, cry out, receive a healing word, and are called to offer thanksgiving sacrifices and joyful testimony. decision_observations.counterevidence: Joining Ps.107.10–22 would make rebellion the organizing criterion, but it would sacrifice the Psalm's intentionally repeated case structure. Prisoners emerge through broken gates; the sick are healed by the sent word and respond at the altar—two complete rescues, not one continuous scene.

decision_observations.support: Seafaring merchants occupy a ten-verse narrative: Yahweh raises the storm, sailors reel and lose courage, they cry, the sea is stilled, they reach the desired haven, and they praise him in the assembly and elders' council. It loses the Psalm's formal distinction between the last refrain cycle, closed publicly at verse 32, and the generalized sayings about Yahweh reversing fortunes from verse 33 onward.

decision_observations.support: Gimel repeats at the start of all eight Hebrew verses from 119:17 through 24 in OSHB and UXLC. decision_observations.support: The Daleth stanza occupies 119:25–32, where all eight Hebrew verses begin with Daleth in OSHB and UXLC. decision_observations.support: Eight He-initial lines fill 119:33–40 in OSHB and UXLC. decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.119.33–48 combines He's petitions with Waw's anticipated answer and is rhetorically attractive. decision_observations.support: OSHB and UXLC each show Waw at the head of all eight Hebrew verses in 119:41–48. Loving kindness and salvation answer reproach, enable a truthful reply, sustain Torah keeping and liberty, and embolden testimony before kings; delight, lifted hands, and meditation finish the stanza before Zayin appears at 49.
decision_observations.counterevidence: A 33–48 merge displays He's petitions followed by Waw's response, but the complementarity depends on recognizing two stanzas rather than dissolving them. decision_observations.support: All lines from 119:49–56 carry Zayin initials in OSHB and UXLC. That devotional pairing is coherent, but verse 57 begins a new eightfold initial and a new pledge; Zayin has already closed by naming command-keeping as the fruit of remembrance.

decision_observations.support: Heth begins each of the eight Hebrew verses in 119:57–64 in OSHB and UXLC. decision_observations.counterevidence: The 49–64 pair connects remembered promise to covenant portion, yet it spans a verified Zayin/Heth change. decision_observations.support: Teth initials repeat through all eight verses of 119:65–72 in OSHB and UXLC. decision_observations.support: Yodh governs the eight Hebrew openings at 119:73–80 in OSHB and UXLC. decision_observations.support: Eight Kaph-initial verses span 119:81–88 in OSHB and UXLC. decision_observations.support: Lamedh is the repeated initial of each Hebrew verse in 119:89–96 in both OSHB and UXLC. decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.119.81–96 creates a powerful Kaph–Lamedh passage from near extinction to enduring word, but the contrast is staged across, not instead of, the alphabetic boundary. decision_observations.support: OSHB and UXLC each show Mem at the head of all eight Hebrew verses from 119:97 to 104. decision_observations.support: Samekh begins all eight Hebrew verses at 119:113–120 in OSHB and UXLC. decision_observations.support: Tsadhe marks each verse from 119:137 through 144 in OSHB and UXLC. decision_observations.support: Resh initials repeat through all eight Hebrew verses of 119:153–160 in OSHB and UXLC. decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.136.23–26 would join need, provision, and final praise, which is a natural closing span. Separating 26 remains useful because it returns to the opening imperative-and-title pattern rather than naming another saving act; the two levels should coexist.

decision_observations.support: The solitary final verse commands thanksgiving to the God of heaven and repeats the refrain one last time. It echoes the opening triad of divine titles after every wonder, creation act, rescue, conquest, remembrance, and provision has been recited, functioning as a closing invocation rather than another catalogue item.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.136.1–26 is mandatory context because a one-verse coda cannot carry the history to which it responds. Still, hiding verse 26 inside the undifferentiated whole loses the Psalm's return from narrated deeds to direct thanksgiving and its final divine title.

decision_observations.support: By Babylon's rivers the exiles sit, weep at Zion's memory, hang their harps, and face captors demanding songs. Their question about singing Yahweh's song in a foreign land completes the scene of coerced performance; verse 5 turns inward to a self-imposed Jerusalem oath.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The complete Ps.137.1–9 is essential, especially because lament, oath, and imprecation belong to one exilic poem. Yet whole-only retrieval suppresses the concrete riverside scene and its closing impossibility question before the speaker changes rhetorical mode.

decision_observations.support: Verses 5–6 form a two-part self-curse: if the speaker forgets Jerusalem, let the right hand lose skill; if Jerusalem is not remembered and exalted above joy, let the tongue cling to the palate. Verse 7 redirects remembrance outward into judgment against Edom.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.137.1–6 unites the setting with the vow it provokes, but it crosses from communal narration and captor demand into first-person oath. The two-verse unit is not arbitrary: matched conditional curses on hand and tongue enact the threatened loss of playing and singing.

decision_observations.support: The remembrance appeal at 137:7 begins the final judgment request against Edom for urging Jerusalem's destruction; Babylon is then addressed as doomed, and two severe beatitudes imagine retaliation. These wishes run without another reset to the Psalm's end.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.137.1–9 prevents the imprecation from being detached from displacement, coercion, and the Jerusalem oath and must be mandatory parent context. The whole, however, should not hide the explicit transition from self-directed remembrance in 5–6 to an appeal concerning Edom and Babylon in 7–9.

decision_observations.support: Yahweh, you have searched me and known me governs 139:1–6: sitting and rising, distant thoughts, paths, words before speech, and divine enclosure accumulate until the speaker confesses such knowledge too wonderful and high to attain. decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.139.1–24 is the indispensable prayer and its final search request deliberately echoes verse 1. Whole-only retrieval, however, would conceal the completed opening meditation on comprehensive knowledge before the poem tests the impossibility of escape.

decision_observations.support: The paired questions Where could I go…Where could I flee? open a survey of heaven, Sheol, dawn's wings, the far sea, and darkness; every imagined destination remains reached and guided by God. Verse 12 concludes that darkness and light are alike to him, while 139:13 begins a causal explanation from bodily formation in the womb.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.139.1–12 joins omniscience and inescapable presence and is a valid larger theological movement. decision_observations.support: Divine formation of the speaker's inmost being at 139:13 grounds praise in womb weaving, fearful and wonderful making, hidden frame, written days, and thoughts too numerous to count. decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.139.13–22 would combine intimate formation with enemy disavowal, perhaps reading both as consequences of divine knowledge. The merge is too coarse for the tonal and speech-act break at 19: praise and wonder give way without transition to imprecation and separation.

decision_observations.support: Verse 19 introduces the wicked and asks God to kill them; bloodthirsty men are told to depart, their hostile use of God's name is charged, and the speaker declares complete hatred of those who rise against Yahweh. decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.139.13–22 would connect God's creative knowledge to the speaker's moral alignment, but it crosses the severe praise-to-imprecation break at 19. Conversely, 19–22 must never be isolated from the full prayer in a way that suppresses the self-examination immediately following it.

decision_observations.support: The final two verses intentionally echo the Psalm's opening by asking God to examine the speaker's heart and thoughts. A further request seeks exposure of any wicked way and guidance in the everlasting way, converting claims about divine knowledge into personal consent and petition.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.139.1–24 is primary because the conclusion's verbs and themes answer the opening declaration. decision_observations.support: Psalm 144 begins by blessing Yahweh for training the king's hands for war and naming him loving kindness, fortress, tower, deliverer, shield, and subduer. The wonder that God notices mortal humanity then contracts life to breath and passing shadow; 144:5 changes from reflection to the imperative Part your heavens…come down.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.144.1–15 remains the complete royal-communal prayer, but whole-only retrieval hides the opening movement from warrior dependence to human frailty. The theophanic commands at verse 5 no longer describe what God is; they ask him to intervene.

decision_observations.support: Part your heavens starts a theophanic rescue plea: descend, touch smoking mountains, flash lightning, shoot arrows, stretch out the hand, and pull the speaker from deep waters and deceitful foreigners. The repeated foreign-hand problem closes at 144:8; verse 9 promises a new ten-string song.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.144.1–8 joins the opening warrior blessing and the intervention it motivates. That larger prayer sequence is valid, but it crosses the 4/5 switch from meditation on breathlike humanity to a concentrated series of divine imperatives.

decision_observations.support: Verse 9 announces a new song on a ten-stringed lyre to the God who gives kings victory and rescues David; verse 11 repeats the request for deliverance from foreigners whose mouths and hands are false. Then our sons… at 144:12 appears to turn from rescue to communal flourishing, although the exact attachment of that result clause remains contestable.
decision_observations.counterevidence: Ps.144.9–15 could read the new song, renewed rescue, and flourishing as one praise-petition-result movement, especially if Then tightly links verse 12 to deliverance. Keeping 9–11 as a child is preferable only as a lower-force seam that acknowledges, rather than erases, that syntactic alternative.

decision_observations.support: From 144:12 the focus becomes communal flourishing: mature sons, sculpted daughters, full storehouses, multiplying flocks, strong cattle, unbreached security, and quiet streets. Two beatitudes close the Psalm by calling such a people happy and finally identifying as happy the people whose God is Yahweh.
decision_observations.counterevidence: The complete Ps.144.1–15 carries the needed chain from warrior dependence and rescue to communal well-being. A 12–15 child can expose the flourishing tableau, but it must not imply that prosperity is detached from the prayer or that the debated Then at 12 is certainly a new independent start.
